executive-function-activities-for-kids:
The games that build executive function are almost all older than any curriculum, and none of them require a worksheet or an app. What they have in common is a specific demand: hold a rule in mind, and stop yourself doing the obvious thing.

What makes an activity count

An activity loads executive function when it asks a child to do at least one of three things: keep something in mind while acting, override an automatic response, or switch between rules. Anything that does none of these is fine to do, but it is not building this.

That is why a memory-matching game counts and a colouring sheet does not, and why a card game where the rule changes counts more than one where it does not.

If the child can do it without thinking, it is not loading the thing you want to load. A little difficulty is the point.

Two to four

  • Simon Says. The purest inhibition game there is: the child must not do the thing they are being told to do. Start easy and speed up.
  • Freeze games. Music stops, everybody freezes. Stopping a body mid-movement is hard, physical inhibition.
  • Sorting. By colour, then by shape, then by size. The switch is where the work is.
  • Pretend play with roles. Holding a role in mind and staying inside it for ten minutes is substantial working-memory work that children do voluntarily.

Four to six

  • Opposites. When I say up, you say down; when I clap once, you clap twice. Then swap the rule mid-game.
  • Memory pairs. Start with six cards, build up. Straightforward working memory, and children will play it for far longer than adults expect.
  • Musical statues and red light green light. Same mechanism as freeze, with more anticipation to hold.
  • Cooking together. A recipe is a multi-step plan held over time, with a real outcome and a reason to keep track.
  • Obstacle courses they design. Planning, sequencing, then executing their own plan, and noticing when it does not work.

Six to eleven

  • Card games with shifting rules. Uno, Crazy Eights, anything where the rule can reverse. The switch cost is the training.
  • Chess, draughts, strategy board games. Holding a plan while responding to somebody else's.
  • Learning an instrument. Among the more demanding everyday activities: attention, inhibition, working memory and delayed reward all at once.
  • Team sports with positions. Holding a role while the situation changes constantly.
  • Cooking a whole meal. Several things finishing at once is genuine planning, and children of nine can do it with less help than they are usually given.

Eleven and up

  • Managing a real budget. Pocket money with genuine trade-offs and no rescue.
  • Planning something backwards. A trip, an event, a piece of coursework, worked back from the deadline.
  • Complex strategy games and Dungeons-and-Dragons style play. Long-horizon planning, rule-holding and perspective-taking together.

Two honest cautions

First: commercial brain-training aimed at these capacities has repeatedly produced improvement on the trained exercise that does not transfer to schoolwork or daily life. Buying a programme is unlikely to be the best use of the money.

Second: the evidence that play-based activities improve executive function is more mixed than enthusiastic write-ups suggest. What is well supported is that sleep, physical activity and complex, sustained, self-directed play are associated with better function. The specific claim that thirty minutes of a particular game produces measurable transfer is not.

The best of these are simply good games played often, with a bit of difficulty in them. That is not a compromise; it is what the evidence actually supports.
how-to-improve-working-memory-in-childre:
Working memory is how much a child can hold in mind while doing something with it. It is small in young children, grows into adolescence, and is the bottleneck almost every school task runs through, which is why so much of what looks like carelessness is actually a capacity running out mid-task.

What it explains

Once you know what working memory is, a set of familiar frustrations stop looking like attitude.

  • The child who goes upstairs and returns with nothing
  • The child who does the first part of an instruction and stops
  • The child who can read every word in a sentence but cannot say what it meant
  • The child who loses their place in a sum halfway through
  • The child who forgets what they were going to say mid-sentence

None of these is a failure of effort. In each one the information has simply dropped out before the task was finished.

Forgetting the second half of an instruction is not defiance. The second half was never held.

Reduce the load before trying to raise the capacity

The capacity grows slowly, on its own timetable. The load, on the other hand, can be changed today, and doing so produces an immediate improvement in what a child can complete.

  • One instruction at a time. The single highest-value change. Four steps become four separate asks, each after the last is done.
  • Put it outside the head. A written list, pictures on the wall, a note on the door. Anything on paper is something that does not have to be held.
  • Ask them to say it back. Not as a test. As a way of moving it from hearing into holding.
  • Automate what can be automated. Number facts and letter sounds that are fully fluent take up no working memory. Time spent making the basics automatic frees capacity for the actual thinking, which is why fluency practice matters more than it looks.
  • Cut the background. Noise and visual clutter consume the same resource the task needs.
  • Give thinking time. Waiting five seconds after a question, without filling the silence, is often all that is needed.

Activities that load it directly

These are games rather than training, and they should be played because they are good games.

  • Memory pairs, building up the number of cards
  • "I went to the shop and I bought…", each player adding an item
  • Following two- and three-step directions in a made-up game
  • Mental arithmetic held aloud rather than written
  • Retelling a story in the right order
  • Learning songs, poems and shlokas by heart

The honest limits

Working memory training has been studied a great deal, and the finding has been consistent and disappointing: children get better at the trained task, and that improvement does not transfer to reading, maths or classroom behaviour. Programmes sold on the promise of transfer are selling something the evidence does not support.

What does help is unremarkable. Sleep, which affects working memory measurably; physical activity; reducing load; and building fluency in the basics so less has to be held at once.

Design around the capacity rather than trying to expand it. That is where the gains actually are.
how-to-teach-self-control-to-children:
Self-control is not obedience, and it cannot be installed by consequences alone. It is a capacity that develops over about two decades, and the adult's job is less to demand it than to create the conditions in which a child gets to practise it and gradually take it over.

Borrowed before it is owned

Very young children have almost no capacity to regulate themselves. What they have instead is an adult who does it for them: the calm voice, the steady body, the predictable response. This is co-regulation, and it is not a lesser version of self-control; it is the developmental route to it.

A child regulates alone by first being regulated with somebody, thousands of times. The internal version is built from the external one.

A child cannot practise calming down in a house where nobody stays calm. They have never seen the thing they are being asked to do.

Roughly how it unfolds

  • Two to four. Almost entirely borrowed. Expect big feelings and very little capacity to hold them. The work is the adult staying steady.
  • Four to six. The first signs of waiting, taking turns, stopping mid-action when reminded. Fragile, and it collapses when tired.
  • Six to eight. More reliable in familiar situations. A child can start to name what they are feeling, which is a significant step.
  • Eight to eleven. Can hold a rule without a reminder much of the time, and can wait for something worth waiting for.
  • Eleven and beyond. Adult-like in calm conditions, and markedly less so among friends, when tired, or when something matters intensely.

What actually builds it

  • Be the calm. The single largest contributor. Your steadiness is the material they are building with.
  • Name it while it is happening. "You are really frustrated with that." Naming a state is the first step to managing it, and children cannot do it for themselves at first.
  • Let them wait, in small doses. Not cruelly, but a child who never waits never practises waiting. Turn-taking games are the easiest version.
  • Rules held consistently. A predictable limit is something a child can organise themselves around. An unpredictable one requires constant vigilance instead.
  • Play that requires it. Board games, team sports, dramatic play with roles. Children exercise more self-control in play they have chosen than in any situation an adult imposes.
  • Protect sleep. Self-control is the first thing to go when a child is short of it.
  • Teach a move, not just a rule. "Come and find me" or "squeeze the cushion" gives a child something to do instead. "Calm down" gives them nothing.

About the marshmallow study

The famous experiment, children who waited for two sweets did better in later life, is worth knowing about mainly because of what came afterwards. Larger replications found the effect much smaller, and substantially explained by family background and circumstances. A child in an environment where promised things do not always arrive is behaving sensibly by taking the sweet now.

The useful lesson is not that early self-control determines a life. It is that self-control depends heavily on whether a child's world has been reliable, which puts the emphasis back on the environment adults build.

You are not teaching a child to suppress themselves. You are lending them your steadiness until they have grown their own.
why-does-my-child-have-trouble-with-tran:
Stopping one thing and starting another is its own skill, and it is harder than either of the activities on either side of it. This is why the child who plays happily and eats happily has a meltdown between the two, and why the same child who is difficult at the table is instantly compliant at the door.

What a transition actually demands

Asking a child to stop and switch requires several things at once, all of them from the slowest-maturing part of their control system.

  • Disengaging. Pulling attention off something absorbing, which is genuinely effortful, and more so the deeper the absorption.
  • Letting go of the plan in their head. A child mid-play usually has an intention: finish this tower, get to the next level. Being stopped means abandoning it, and they often cannot explain that is what has upset them.
  • Tolerating the drop. Moving from something interesting to something dull is a real fall in state, and small children feel it sharply.
  • Loading the new thing. Working out what is now expected, while still holding the disappointment.

The meltdown is rarely about the bath. It is about being taken out of something mid-thought.

What helps most

  • Warn, in their units. "Two more turns" or "when this song finishes" works far better than "five minutes", which is meaningless to a young child. The warning lets them finish internally rather than being cut off.
  • Go to them. A transition announced across a room is often not received at all. Close, at eye level, waiting for them to look.
  • Give the ending a shape. The same phrase, the same small ritual, every time. Predictable endings become bearable endings.
  • Preserve the work. "We can leave the tower up" removes most of the objection, which was never about stopping but about losing.
  • Point at what comes next. A transition towards something is easier than a transition away from something.
  • Keep the order fixed. A sequence that never varies stops being a series of decisions and becomes one automatic run.
  • Let them run it. "What comes after teeth?" hands the sequence over. A child who leads the transition resists it far less.

Screens are a harder case

Ending screen time combines a hard transition with an unusually absorbing state, which is why it produces reactions out of proportion to anything else in the day. The same tools work, with more of them: a warning, a natural stopping point rather than a mid-level cut, and something specific to move to.

When transitions are unusually hard

Some children find them consistently harder than their peers, across settings and well past the age where most have eased. Where that comes with strong routine preferences, distress at small changes, or sensory sensitivities, it is worth mentioning to somebody who can observe your child directly, not because it means something is wrong, but because the strategies that help are more specific and worth having.

Transitions are not a behaviour problem with a discipline answer. They are a skill, and they respond to warning, ritual and practice.

This piece is general guidance and is not a substitute for an assessment by someone who knows your child.
